\title{How much junk do rules catch?\\
pygarble on real survey responses and social-media text}
\author{Ujjwal Singh Rao\\
\small \TODO{affiliation}\\

\begin{abstract}
Free-text fields collect junk: keyboard mashing, random strings and
placeholder answers. pygarble is a Python library with no runtime
dependencies that flags such text with rules and small embedded English
statistics. We measure it on two public datasets against a Markov-chain
gibberish detector and a language identifier, with every method at its
own default decision. On \nA{} survey responses labelled as junk,
pygarble's \code{english\_fusion} profile flags
\res{english_fusion}{A_capture}. On \nB{} English rows of random strings
and tweets, it recalls \res{english_fusion}{B_recall} of the random
strings with precision \res{english_fusion}{B_precision}, from a
\mb{english_fusion}\,MB install. A post hoc variant of the default profile
without its two encoding-damage checks shows that the ensemble can be
adapted to a domain by removing strategies: its false-positive rate on
tweets falls from \respct{english}{B_fpr}\,\% to
\respct{english_tuned}{B_fpr}\,\% with no loss of recall. We report where
each method is beaten, its cost, and which configuration to use for which
job.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

Text pipelines receive junk. Survey free-text questions get keyboard
mashing from respondents who want to reach the next page. Sign-up forms get
random strings from bots. Scraped text carries encoding damage. Each of
these costs something downstream: a coder reads it, a model is trained on
it, or an analysis counts it as an answer.

The usual remedies are heavy. A language model or a trained classifier
needs a model download, a GPU or an API call, and its decisions are hard
to explain row by row. Simple rules are cheap, local and explainable, and
are often the first filter a team writes by hand. The question is how much
junk such rules actually catch, and how much good text they wrongly flag.

pygarble \citep{pygarble} packages rules of this kind: character and
word statistics computed against embedded English tables, with no runtime
dependencies. This paper measures it on real data rather than on examples
written by its author. \TODO{one or two sentences on the maintainer's own
motivating use case.}

The contributions are:
\begin{itemize}
\item A benchmark on two public datasets: \nA{} survey responses labelled
  as junk, and \nB{} English rows of random strings and tweets. Every
  method runs at its own default decision. The protocol, a pilot run and
  every change after it are disclosed, and per-row predictions are saved so
  every number can be recomputed.
\item A comparison of pygarble's default profile and its
  \code{english\_fusion} profile with two CPU baselines: a character
  Markov-chain gibberish detector and a language identifier.
\item A post hoc, domain-specific tuning of the default profile, reported
  separately from the main results.
\item The cost of each method, a plain account of where pygarble is
  beaten, and guidance on which configuration to use.
\end{itemize}

\section{pygarble in one page}

pygarble targets Python 3.8 and later and has no runtime dependencies. The
installed package, with its embedded English tables, is
\mb{english_fusion}\,MB. Besides gibberish detection it scans text for
secrets, personal data and profanity, with redaction; those features are
not evaluated here.

\paragraph{Strategies.} Gibberish detection is built from
\nstrategies{} strategies, each a function from text to a score in
$[0,1]$ and a decision. They fall into a few groups: character statistics
(vowel ratio, entropy, consonant runs, letter frequency); English
character models (a Markov chain, bigram and trigram tables, a
log-likelihood ratio against a uniform reference); word-level checks
(dictionary lookup, word anomaly, function-word density); structural checks
(repetition, keyboard rows and adjacency, hex strings); encoding checks
(mojibake, control characters, Unicode script mixing); and four checks
that compare a text window with frequent English (cross parsing, primed
compression, n-gram rank and a permutation test). Each strategy reports
when it does not apply, for example to text with no Latin letters.

\paragraph{Ensembles and profiles.} \code{EnsembleDetector} combines a
named set of strategies, a \emph{profile}, under a voting rule, and flags a
text when the combined score reaches the threshold, 0.5 by default. Two
profiles are measured here:
\begin{itemize}
\item \code{english}, the default: Markov chain, log-likelihood ratio, word
  anomaly, mojibake, keyboard adjacency and control characters, with
  \code{any} voting, so one member firing flags the text.
\item \code{english\_fusion}, opt-in: word lookup, log-likelihood ratio and
  cross parsing with \code{fisher} voting. Each member's score is read
  against that member's scores on a synthetic English null built from word
  frequencies, and the tail probabilities are combined with Fisher's
  method.
\end{itemize}
The other profiles, a larger English set, the 0.8.0 set and profiles for
encoding damage, Unicode spoofing and degenerate model output, are not
measured here. A user can also pass any list of
strategies, which is how the tuned variant in
Section~\ref{sec:tuning} is built.

\paragraph{What it is not.} The English profiles score English
plausibility. They are not language identifiers: meaningful text in other
languages written in Latin letters can be flagged, and text in other
scripts gives them no signal. Scores are heuristic, not calibrated
probabilities. A \code{calibrate()} helper picks a threshold from a user's
own labelled examples; this paper does not use it.

\section{Datasets and protocol}

\paragraph{A: survey junk.} The Kaggle dataset
\code{johnwdata/\allowbreak gibberish-text-classification} \citep{dataA} has
\nArows{} survey responses, all labelled as junk. Despite its
\code{.xls} extension, the file is a Windows-1252 CSV. We strip each
response, drop empty ones and drop exact duplicates, leaving \nA{} rows.
A has no clean rows, so the only metric is the \emph{capture rate}: the
share of rows a method flags. Its licence is listed as unknown, so the
repository stores row indices and hashes, never the text.

\paragraph{B: random strings and tweets.} We pool the train, validation
and test files of the Hugging Face dataset
\code{Sowmya15/gibberish\_multilingual} \citep{dataB} (Apache-2.0) and
keep the \nB{} non-empty rows whose language is English: \nBpos{} random strings (junk) and \nBneg{} tweets
(clean). Labels are used as given and duplicates are kept (\nBdup{} rows
repeat an earlier text). We report precision, recall and the
false-positive rate (FPR), the share of tweets flagged.

\paragraph{Methods.} pygarble 0.11.0 is used with its defaults frozen at
commit \code{e3135ed}; no default or threshold was changed after any
result was seen. The baselines run on CPU with pinned versions:
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{gibberish-detector} 0.1.1 \citep{gibberishdetector}, a
  character Markov model. The package ships no model, so we train one with
  its own trainer on the corpus its README uses, and flag scores above its
  command-line default of 4.0.
\item \textbf{lingua} 2.2.0 \citep{lingua}, a language identifier, under
  the policy ``not detected as English is junk''.
\end{itemize}
There are no neural baselines.

\paragraph{Decision and intervals.} Every method is scored at its own
default decision: the binary output it gives with default settings. No
threshold is fitted on either dataset. Intervals are 95\,\% percentile
intervals from \resamples{} bootstrap resamples of rows, drawn with a fixed
seed and shared by all methods.

\paragraph{Pilot and changes.} Before the protocol was written, all of A
and all English rows of B were scored once with pygarble's defaults. The
\code{english\_fusion} numbers from that pilot are the ones reported here,
because nothing in the package changed afterwards. The first version of
the protocol also fitted thresholds at fixed false-positive rates on a
development split of B and compared more baselines and pygarble
configurations; both were computed and then removed from the paper's
scope (Section~\ref{sec:limitations}). The tuned variant in
Section~\ref{sec:tuning} was added after the results were seen.

\code{english\_fusion} flags \res{english_fusion}{A_capture} of the real

by calling anything it cannot identify as English junk, a policy whose

\section{Results on social-media text}
\label{sec:social}

On B, \code{english\_fusion} recalls \res{english_fusion}{B_recall} of the
random strings with precision \res{english_fusion}{B_precision}
(Figure~\ref{fig:results}, right). It flags
\respct{english_fusion}{B_fpr}\,\% of tweets. lingua has similar recall
(\res{lingua}{B_recall}) and lower precision
(\res{lingua}{B_precision}). gibberish-detector has the highest precision,
\res{gibberish_detector}{B_precision}, and the lowest recall,
\res{gibberish_detector}{B_recall}. The default \code{english} profile
recalls \res{english}{B_recall} with precision \res{english}{B_precision}.

A note on what counts as a false positive. \mojibakepct\,\% of the tweets
in B contain mojibake byte signatures, for example a UTF-8 emoji decoded
as Latin-1. B labels these tweets clean, because it was built to
separate random strings from tweets. A pipeline that audits encoding would
want them flagged.

\subsection{Domain-specific tuning}
\label{sec:tuning}

The default \code{english} profile includes two strategies that target
encoding damage: mojibake and control characters. The second fires on the
C1 control characters inside mojibake. Since this dataset labels encoding
damage as clean, a user screening social-media text for gibberish would
drop both. We built that variant: the \code{english} profile without
mojibake and control characters, with the same \code{any} voting and
threshold. The package was not changed.

This variant was constructed after seeing that \mojibakepct\,\% of the
tweets carry mojibake and that these strategies flag them. It is post hoc
and reported as such, not as a pre-registered result. Its results next to
the untuned profile:

\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{lllll}
\toprule
& A capture & B precision & B recall & B FPR \\
\midrule
\code{english} & \res{english}{A_capture} & \res{english}{B_precision}
  & \res{english}{B_recall} & \res{english}{B_fpr} \\
\code{english}, tuned & \res{english_tuned}{A_capture}
  & \res{english_tuned}{B_precision} & \res{english_tuned}{B_recall}
  & \res{english_tuned}{B_fpr} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

Capture on A and recall on B are unchanged, because no junk row in either
dataset depended on the two encoding checks. Precision rises and the FPR
on tweets falls. The point is not this particular variant but that the
ensemble can be adapted to a domain by removing strategies whose target
the domain does not treat as junk. \code{english\_fusion} has no mojibake
member, so it has no such variant.

\section{Where it fails}
\label{sec:fails}

\paragraph{False positives.} The Markov baseline,
gibberish-detector, flags \respct{gibberish_detector}{B_fpr}\,\% of tweets;
\code{english\_fusion} flags \respct{english_fusion}{B_fpr}\,\%.

\paragraph{The default profile on informal text.} The default
\code{english} profile flags \respct{english}{B_fpr}\,\% of tweets. Tuning
lowers this to \respct{english_tuned}{B_fpr}\,\%, still above
\code{english\_fusion}.

\paragraph{Language identification captures more survey junk.} lingua
flags \res{lingua}{A_capture} of A against fusion's
\res{english_fusion}{A_capture}, at an FPR of \respct{lingua}{B_fpr}\,\% on
tweets and a \mb{lingua}\,MB install.

\paragraph{Short inputs, digits and repetition.} \code{english\_fusion}
misses \nAmissedfusion{} of the \nA{} rows in A. On inspection, many are
one to three characters long. Most of the rest mix letters with digits,
contain no letters at all, or repeat a short syllable or a punctuation
mark. Some are real words or short phrases, which read as English to
character and word statistics.

\paragraph{Label noise in A.} A is used as labelled. \nAmissedall{} rows
are flagged by none of the four untuned methods. On inspection many are
meaningful but low-effort answers, such as thanks or a short positive
phrase, so A's capture rates have a ceiling below one.

\paragraph{B is easy.} B's junk is random character strings, which share
almost nothing with English; fusion and lingua recall
\res{english_fusion}{B_recall} and \res{lingua}{B_recall} of them. B therefore says little about recall on realistic junk and mostly
measures false positives on informal English.

\section{Guidance}

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Screening survey or form free text:} \code{english\_fusion}.
  It catches \res{english_fusion}{A_capture} of real survey junk and
  \res{english_fusion}{B_recall} of random strings, at
  \ms{english_fusion}\,ms per 1,000 texts, from a
  \mb{english_fusion}\,MB install with no dependencies. Add a
  minimum-length rule if one- and two-character answers count as junk.
\item \textbf{Adapting to a domain:} start from a profile and remove the
  strategies whose target the domain does not treat as junk, as in
  Section~\ref{sec:tuning}. For social-media text, drop mojibake and
  control characters unless encoding damage is itself a concern.
\item \textbf{When false positives cost much more than misses:} at
  default settings, gibberish-detector flags the fewest tweets.
\item \textbf{Multilingual input:} route by language first. A language
  identifier answers that question; it is not a junk detector.
\end{itemize}

\section{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

Two public datasets are measured, both English. A has only junk, so it
measures capture and nothing about false positives; B's junk is random
strings, which are easier than real junk. Both datasets are short texts;
pygarble's behaviour on long documents is not measured here. There is no
neural baseline, and only two baselines. A comparison at a matched
false-positive rate was computed in PR~18 and removed from the paper's
scope; in it the Markov baseline captured more survey junk than
\code{english\_fusion}. It remains in the repository history.
Each method is run once at its default decision, so the results say how
the methods behave out of the box, not how well they can be tuned. The one
tuned variant is post hoc and was chosen with knowledge of B.

\section{Reproducibility}

The benchmark code is in \code{paper/scripts/benchmark/}, the protocol and
every deviation from it in \code{paper/benchmark/}, and results in
\code{paper/benchmark/results/}. The manifest records the sha256 hash of
each raw file (for A, beginning \code{\shaA}) and every row id; no dataset
text is committed. Per-row scores and decisions for every method are
committed, so every number in this paper can be recomputed without the
raw data:
\begin{verbatim}
make benchmark-verify PYTHON=<venv>/bin/python
make preprint PYTHON=<venv>/bin/python
\end{verbatim}
The first command recomputes \code{metrics.json} from the saved predictions
and fails on any difference. The second regenerates the figure, the
tables and the number macros this paper is typeset from, then builds the
PDF. Re-scoring from the raw files is described in
\code{paper/\allowbreak scripts/\allowbreak benchmark/\allowbreak README.md}; scores are deterministic.
